title: Assessing Active and Passive Glenohumeral Rotational Deficits in Professional Tennis Players: Normative Values at 90 and 45 of Abduction for Making Decisions in Injury Prevention Programs
content: (1) Background: Glenohumeral internal and external rotational range of movement (GIRD and GERD) has been considered one of the primary outcomes to determine risk of injury in overhead athletes, as tennis players. Nevertheless, current testing position doesn’t consider than most tennis actions are repeated at 45of abduction, and actively. The aim of this study is establishing normative values of pathological GIRD and GERD in tennis players, to estimate the passive and active range of motion of the glenohumeral joint at 90° and 45º of abduction.; (2) Methods: 43 tennis players voluntarily participated in the study (19.1±2.75 years). Dominant and non-dominant shoulder range of motion (ROM), external rotation (ER), internal rotation (IR) at 90 and 45 in active and passive conditions were evaluated. GIRD and GERD were calculated in both positions and conditions; (3) Results: There were significant differences for all passive measurements between 45 and 90 testing position. ER and TROM at 90 and 45 showed significant differences in both passive and active conditions and in the dominant and non-dominant side. There were no significant differences in IR and TROM actively in both the dominant and the non-dominant at 90 or 45; (4) Conclusions: It is necessary to evaluate the ER under the same conditions at 90 or 45. Practitioners should consider assessing ER at the angle at which most actions are repeated in tennis (45°) as a method to monitor GERD. Evaluating GERD in asymptomatic tennis players could help avoid future biomechanical and GIRD problems. Both GIRD and GERD should be considered as a percentage of the athlete's own deficit in IR or ER, instead of having as a reference specific degree that have been observed in baseball pitchers.
